\chapter{What the Body Tells You}
\label{ch:hi-what-the-body-tells-you}
\hlchaptermodality{63}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what my body is telling me when someone asks how I am.}

Complete HI-C63-pain and say all five words in order.

\section[bhūkh]{\hi{भूख} (bhūkh) — hunger}

\label{lesson:HI-C63-hunger}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{lakṛī} mean, and what did \emph{miṭṭī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{भूख}}
\textbf{\hi{भूख}} (\emph{bhūkh}) — \textquotedblleft{}hunger\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{बुभुक्षा} (\emph{bubhukṣā}), 'the wish to eat', built on \hi{भुज्} (\emph{bhuj-}), 'to eat, to enjoy'. The old form doubles its own first syllable, which is how Sanskrit marked wanting to do a thing rather than doing it.

So \hi{भूख} was never the state of an empty stomach — it was the appetite, the wanting. A speaker says \hi{भूख} belongs to them rather than that they are it, and the wanting is the thing that is owned.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things a body reports.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhūkh}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bhūkh}, then \emph{roṭī}, and say which one settles the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{भूख} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}hunger\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pyās]{\hi{प्यास} (pyās) — thirst}

\label{lesson:HI-C63-thirst}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bhūkh} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{प्यास}}
\textbf{\hi{प्यास}} (\emph{pyās}) — \textquotedblleft{}thirst\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{पिपासा} (\emph{pipāsā}), 'the wish to drink', on \hi{पा} (\emph{pā-}), 'to drink' — and doubling its first syllable exactly the way \hi{बुभुक्षा} does. The two words were made in the same workshop on the same day.

\hi{पा} is the root under \hi{पानी}, the word you have had since the water lesson: 'the drinkable one'. So \hi{प्यास} and \hi{पानी} are the wanting and the thing wanted, cut from a single syllable.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pyās}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pyās}, then \emph{pānī}, and say which one ends the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{प्यास} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}thirst\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nīnd]{\hi{नींद} (nīnd) — sleep}

\label{lesson:HI-C63-sleep}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pyās} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{नींद}}
\textbf{\hi{नींद}} (\emph{nīnd}) — \textquotedblleft{}sleep\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{निद्रा} (\emph{nidrā}), 'sleep'. The \emph{r} went, the vowel picked up the nose-mark you learnt to write, and \hi{निद्रा} turned into \hi{नींद} without changing its meaning by a hair.

It patterns with \hi{भूख} and \hi{प्यास}: a speaker says \hi{नींद} is coming to them, not that they are sleepy. Three states in a row that Hindi treats as visitors rather than as things you are.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nīnd}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nīnd}, then \emph{rāt}, and say which one brings the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{नींद} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sleep\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bukhār]{\hi{बुख़ार} (bukhār) — a fever}

\label{lesson:HI-C63-fever}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nīnd} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बुख़ार}}
\textbf{\hi{बुख़ार}} (\emph{bukhār}) — \textquotedblleft{}a fever\textquotedblright{}.

An Arabic word, \emph{bukhār}, that came in through Persian. Its plain sense is steam or vapour — the mist that comes off hot water.

Older medicine pictured a fever as exactly that: a vapour rising inside a body. The picture was wrong and the word stayed, which happens more often than not. Note the dot under the \hi{ख़}, the same dot you have already met inside \hi{ख़ुशी}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bukhār}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bukhār}, then \emph{ṭhīk}, and say which one you would rather report
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बुख़ार} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a fever\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dard]{\hi{दर्द} (dard) — pain}

\label{lesson:HI-C63-pain}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{दर्द}}
\textbf{\hi{दर्द}} (\emph{dard}) — \textquotedblleft{}pain\textquotedblright{}.

A Persian word, \emph{dard}, and it is usually traced to a very old root meaning 'to split, to tear' — the same root that surfaces in English \emph{tear}, in the sense of ripping cloth.

\hi{दर्द} covers the ache in a \hi{घुटना} and the grief in a chest with one word, and Urdu poetry leans on that double reach so hard that the word now sounds a little literary even when it is plainly medical.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{भूख}, \hi{प्यास}, \hi{नींद}, \hi{बुख़ार}, \hi{दर्द}. Enough to answer honestly when someone asks how you are.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dard}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{ṭhīk}, if you are
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{दर्द} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}pain\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
